sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe cell structure and function, including the roles of major organelles and membrane transport.
- Identify the four primary tissue types and their characteristics, locations, and functions.
- Explain homeostasis and how negative and positive feedback loops maintain a stable internal environment.
- Relate basic cellular and tissue changes to health and disease.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

The plasma membrane is like a security gate at a building entrance. It is the outer wall, and the gatekeeper decides which things may come in and which must stay out.

### Question 2

The nucleus is like the control room of a factory. It keeps the master instruction book (DNA) that tells the whole cell what to build and do.

### Question 3

Cytoplasm is like the water inside a fish tank. It fills the space, holds the parts in place, and lets things float and move around inside the cell.

### Question 4

Mitochondria are like tiny power plants inside the cell. They burn fuel and make the energy (ATP) that the cell uses to do its jobs.

### Question 5

Ribosomes are like the assembly workers in a factory. They take instructions and snap small pieces (amino acids) together to make big protein products.

### Question 6

The rough ER is like a kitchen counter covered in workers (ribosomes) who assemble meals (proteins) and then tidy them up before sending them out.

### Question 7

The Golgi apparatus is like a post office. It takes packages (proteins), adds labels, and sorts them into boxes headed to the right addresses.

### Question 8

Lysosomes are like the recycling and trash team inside a factory. They take broken parts and garbage and break them down so the cell stays clean and can reuse the pieces.

### Question 9

The cell's outer skin is like a double-layered sandwich made of special fat-like molecules. This sandwich is strong enough to be a wall but flexible enough to let some things pass.

### Question 10

Diffusion is like a drop of food coloring spreading out in a glass of water. It moves by itself from the crowded spot to the empty spots, with no one pushing it.

### Question 11

Osmosis is just the special name for water moving by itself across a wall. Water slides toward the side that is more crowded with dissolved stuff, trying to even things out.

### Question 12

Active transport is like walking up an escalator that is moving down. It takes extra effort (energy) because you are going against the flow instead of riding with it.

### Question 13

Riding a bike downhill takes no pedaling (passive), but riding uphill you have to pedal hard and use energy (active). The cell works the same way.

### Question 14

ATP is like the batteries that power a toy. When the toy runs, the battery gives off energy, and when it is empty it must be recharged. ATP is the cell's rechargeable battery.

### Question 15

Chromosomes are like neatly folded instruction books kept on a shelf in the nucleus. Each book holds many recipes (genes) the body needs.

### Question 16

A gene is like a single recipe inside a big cookbook (a chromosome). Each recipe tells the cell how to make one specific protein.

### Question 17

Mitosis is like photocopying one worksheet into two identical copies. Both new copies match the original exactly.

### Question 18

Gas exchange is like two rooms with a door open. If one room has more people, some wander into the emptier room until both are balanced, all by themselves.

### Question 19

Imagine a raisin. If the water around it is saltier than the inside, water leaks out of the raisin toward the salt, making it shrivel even smaller.

### Question 20

A sprinter needs lots of food for energy, so their kitchen (mitochondria) is huge. Busy muscle cells pack in many power plants because they burn energy nonstop.

### Question 21

Making a protein to ship out is like an assembly line: workers (ribosomes) build it, a finishing station (Golgi) wraps it, and the loading dock (membrane) sends it out the door.

### Question 22

Differentiation is like students growing up to pick different jobs. One becomes a builder, another a chef. Each cell learns a specific job and takes the right tools for it.

### Question 23

A stem cell is like a blank, unshaped piece of clay. Depending on what it becomes, it can be molded into many different finished figures.

### Question 24

Exocytosis and endocytosis are like a package delivery truck. Goods are loaded into a box (vesicle) and either driven out the gate or brought in through it.

### Question 25

Cellular respiration is like a furnace. It burns fuel (glucose) with oxygen to release heat and power for the house (ATP).

### Question 26

Facilitated diffusion is like a turnstile that lets people walk into a stadium. The crowd naturally flows from the busy side to the empty side, and the turnstile just gives them a doorway.

### Question 27

Cilia are like thousands of tiny brooms on a cell that sweep dust and mucus along in one direction, keeping passageways clean.

### Question 28

The cytoskeleton is like the steel frame and scaffolding inside a building. It holds the shape, keeps rooms in place, and lets things move along tracks.

### Question 29

The smooth ER is like a chemistry lab that makes fats and oils and helps clean up harmful chemicals, a different job from the rough ER's protein kitchen next door.

### Question 30

A tissue is like a team of workers who all do the same job. Many similar cells team up to do one task, like covering a surface or moving a muscle.

### Question 31

The body has four main teams of cells: coverers (epithelial), connectors and supporters (connective), movers (muscle), and messengers (nervous).

### Question 32

Epithelial tissue is like the wallpaper and floor covering of the body. It lines surfaces, protects what is underneath, and some of it even oozes helpful fluids.

### Question 33

The top layer of your skin is like the protective wrapper on a package. That wrapping is epithelial tissue, not the moving muscles or the stretchy cords underneath.

### Question 34

Connective tissue is like the glue, ropes, and padding in a house. It holds things together, fills gaps, and cushions and protects the important parts.

### Question 35

Bone, blood, and cartilage are all part of the body's support-and-delivery team. Even though blood looks liquid, it is a connective tissue because its cells float in a liquid matrix.

### Question 36

Muscle tissue is the body's engine. It shortens and pulls to make things move, whether you are running or your stomach is squeezing food along.

### Question 37

There are three kinds of muscle: the ones you control to move your body (skeletal), the one that beats your heart (cardiac), and the ones that quietly squeeze your organs (smooth).

### Question 38

Skeletal muscle is the kind you can flex on purpose, like your arm muscles. Under a microscope it has stripes, and it pulls on your bones to move you.

### Question 39

Cardiac muscle is the special muscle that pumps your heart all day and night without you telling it to. It has stripes but runs on autopilot.

### Question 40

Smooth muscle is the quiet worker inside your blood vessels and digestive tract. It squeezes things along automatically, and it has no stripes.

### Question 41

Nervous tissue is the body's telephone wiring. It sends fast electrical messages so the brain can tell the rest of the body what to do in an instant.

### Question 42

A neuron is like a telephone wire in the body. It carries the electric message from one place to another so the body can react quickly.

### Question 43

Neuroglia are like the support crew backstage at a concert. They do not sing (send signals), but they feed, protect, and clean up so the star performers (neurons) can do their job.

### Question 44

Stratified squamous is like a thick stack of flat paving tiles. Many flat layers stacked up make a tough, protective surface, like the skin or the lining of the mouth.

### Question 45

Glandular epithelium is like the sprinkler system of the body. These cells make and squirt out helpful fluids such as sweat, mucus, and hormones.

### Question 46

Blood is like a watery soup with cells floating in it. Because the cells float in a liquid 'glue' (plasma) instead of being packed tightly together, we call it a connective tissue.

### Question 47

Adipose tissue is the body's padding and blanket. It stores fuel, keeps you warm, and acts like bubble wrap around your organs.

### Question 48

The inside of your mouth is covered by a smooth lining, like the lining of a coat. That lining is epithelial tissue, the body's cover-and-line team.

### Question 49

Tendons and ligaments are like strong ropes and cables that tie muscles and bones together. Ropes are connective tissue, not skin or nerves.

### Question 50

Your heart is a muscular pump, and the special muscle that builds it is cardiac muscle. It works nonstop without you thinking about it.

### Question 51

The brain and spinal cord are the body's supercomputer and main cable, built from messenger cells (nervous tissue) rather than muscle or fat.

### Question 52

Mucous membranes are the wet, slippery linings of your nose, mouth, and gut. They are like the damp inner coating of a garden hose, while your outer skin is the dry cover.

### Question 53

Regeneration is like fixing a broken toy with the exact same part so it works again. Fibrosis is like patching the toy with tape; it is held together but may not work the same way.

### Question 54

Connective tissue is like a fruit salad with lots of jelly. The fruit pieces (cells) sit far apart in a big bowl of jelly (matrix), while epithelial cells stand packed shoulder to shoulder like bricks in a wall.

### Question 55

Homeostasis is like a house thermostat keeping the rooms at a comfy temperature no matter how hot or cold it is outside. Your body does the same for its inside conditions.

### Question 56

A feedback loop is like a smoke detector system: the sensor (receptor) smells smoke, the alarm panel (control center) decides what to do, and the sprinkler (effector) sprays water.

### Question 57

Negative feedback is like a boat that starts to tip, so you lean the other way to straighten it. The body pushes back against changes to keep things level.

### Question 58

Positive feedback is like a snowball rolling downhill: it gets bigger and faster as it goes, building on itself until the job is done.

### Question 59

When you get too hot, your body turns on the fans (sweat) and opens the windows (widened blood vessels) to cool you back down. That is the body pushing back to normal.

### Question 60

When your blood sugar goes up after eating, insulin works like a cleanup crew to bring it back down. The body pushes the number back to normal, like a thermostat.

### Question 61

If your blood pressure climbs too high, your body sends a message to slow the heart and widen the pipes to bring the pressure back down, like easing off a hose.

### Question 62

A set point is like the temperature you set on a thermostat. It is the 'just right' number your body tries to keep things close to.

### Question 63

Your home thermostat is a mini version of your body's control system. It checks the temperature and turns the heat or air on to bring the room back to the setting you chose.

### Question 64

Childbirth is like a snowball of squeezing that keeps building. Each squeeze triggers a bigger squeeze until the baby is born, with the signal getting stronger and stronger.

### Question 65

Clotting is like a snowball of helpers: the first platelets call more friends, who call even more, until a solid plug forms to stop the bleeding.

### Question 66

Negative feedback is like a boat's stabilizer pushing back to keep it level. Positive feedback is like a snowball that keeps growing bigger as it rolls.

### Question 67

The receptor is like the smoke detector in a house. Its job is to notice that something has changed and sound the alarm for the rest of the system.

### Question 68

The effector is like the sprinkler that actually sprays water after the smoke alarm goes off. It is the part that does the fixing.

### Question 69

The control center is like the alarm panel that decides what to do after a sensor goes off. It takes the message and tells the right part to act.

### Question 70

A fever is like someone turning the house thermostat up on purpose, then turning it back down. When it goes back down, the house is too warm, so the air conditioning (sweating) kicks on.

### Question 71

Shivering is your body's built-in heater. When you are cold, your muscles shake quickly on purpose to warm you up, like rubbing your hands together.

### Question 72

Sweat is like water sprayed on your skin on a hot day. As the water dries (evaporates), it pulls heat away and cools you down.

### Question 73

When blood sugar climbs too high, the pancreas sends out insulin like a cleanup crew to bring the number back down to the 'just right' level.

### Question 74

When the body's balance system breaks, things go wrong, like a thermostat that stops working and lets the house get too hot. Many illnesses are the body's balance getting out of whack.

### Question 75

If a bucket is leaking, you stop pouring water out and try to save what is left. The body does the same, making less urine to hold onto water when it is losing too much.

### Question 76

When you run, your muscles need more fuel and air, so your body speeds up the heart and lungs to pump extra oxygen in and carry waste out, like turning up a machine under load.

### Question 77

If someone has been out in the cold and is shaking and confused, that is a red flag. The assistant's job is to call for help from the nurse or doctor right away, like pulling a fire alarm.

### Question 78

Cells are like tiny engines that need oxygen to run. If the oxygen supply is cut off, the engine sputters and can get damaged.

### Question 79

Atrophy is like a muscle that gets smaller when it is not used for a long time, like a balloon slowly losing air.

### Question 80

Hypertrophy is like a muscle getting bigger because each of its cells grows larger, like balloons being blown up more, not by adding more balloons.

### Question 81

Hyperplasia is like a team getting bigger by adding more players, while hypertrophy is the same players getting stronger. Hyperplasia means more cells.

### Question 82

Neoplasia is like a factory line that keeps making extra products when it should stop, piling up a lump. Some piles stay put (benign) and some spread (malignant).

### Question 83

Inflammation is like the body sounding an alarm and sending helpers to a boo-boo. The area gets red, warm, puffy, and sore while the repair crew works.

### Question 84

If you see a strange new spot that is growing, you do not guess what it is. You write it down and tell the doctor or nurse, who knows what to do next.
